stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Folklorists have long assumed that riddles passed down by word of mouth change quickly as they move from one teller to the next. To test this, researcher Amara Okafor recorded the same twelve riddles from grandparents and their grandchildren in three Ghanaian villages. More than 80 percent of the riddles were worded almost identically across the two generations. Oral riddles, her findings suggest, can be far more stable than scholars had believed.
choices: To describe a study whose results challenge a common assumption about how oral riddles change over time
To describe a study that was unable to determine whether oral riddles change from one generation to the next
To compare the riddles told in three Ghanaian villages with riddles collected in other parts of the world
To explain why grandchildren prefer to repeat riddles in exactly the words their grandparents once used
explanation: The text opens with an old belief (riddles change quickly), then describes Okafor's recordings and ends with a clear result: the riddles stayed nearly identical. So the text describes a study, and that study's findings challenge the assumption. Choice A names both parts.

B.why: You saw 'describe a study' and stopped reading. The text gives a clear result: over 80 percent of the riddles matched. The question was answered, not left open.

C.why: You picked a comparison, but the text never mentions riddles from anywhere else. It only reports what Okafor found in the three villages.

D.why: You read a motive into the findings. The study shows that the wording stayed the same. It says nothing about what the grandchildren prefer or why they repeat the riddles that way.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: An earthquake sends out two main kinds of waves. Primary waves are fast but usually cause little damage, while secondary waves travel more slowly and do most of the shaking. Earthquake early-warning systems take advantage of this gap. Sensors near the fault detect the primary waves, computers estimate the quake's location and strength within seconds, and alerts go out to phones before the secondary waves arrive.
choices: To explain how early-warning systems use the difference between two waves to alert people before strong shaking
To describe the method that computers use to estimate an earthquake's location from the data that sensors collect
To compare primary and secondary waves in order to show which kind is more dangerous to buildings and people
To argue that earthquake early-warning systems are too slow to give people any useful notice before shaking
explanation: The text sets up a fact (fast, weak waves and slow, damaging waves) and then walks through each step of a warning system that uses that gap: detect, estimate, alert. Choice A names the whole mechanism.

B.why: You took one step of the process for the whole thing. Estimating the quake's location is only the middle step. The text is about how the full system turns the gap between the waves into a warning.

C.why: This is the comparison trap. The text does contrast the two waves, but only as setup. Its main job is explaining the warning system, not ranking which wave is more dangerous.

D.why: You read an evaluation into a text that only explains. The text says the alerts arrive before the secondary waves, which is the opposite of 'too slow.'

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Many Japanese woodblock prints from the nineteenth century feature a striking blue, but art historians have long been unsure which pigment produced it: the traditional plant dye indigo or the imported synthetic Prussian blue. Because the two pigments reflect infrared light differently, a team of conservators scanned forty prints with an infrared camera. The scans revealed Prussian blue in nearly every print made after 1830.
choices: To describe an analysis that answered a long-standing question about the blue pigment used in certain prints
To describe an analysis that left open the question of which blue pigment printers used in certain prints
To argue that prints made with indigo were more vivid and long-lasting than prints made with Prussian blue
To explain the steps that nineteenth-century Japanese printers followed when carving their woodblocks
explanation: The passage announces an open question (indigo or Prussian blue?), describes the infrared scans, and ends with a clear answer: Prussian blue in nearly every print after 1830. Choice A gets both the method and the result right.

B.why: You matched 'describe an analysis' and missed the end of the choice. The last sentence gives a definite finding, so the question was not left open.

C.why: You read a judgment into a report. The text never compares how vivid or long-lasting the two pigments are. It only identifies which one was used.

D.why: You latched onto the topic of woodblock printing. The text never describes carving. It is about identifying a pigment.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Sea cucumbers are often treated as passive scavengers that simply drift across the seafloor eating debris. Marine biologist Lena Varga, however, placed sea cucumbers in tanks of reef sediment and measured the sediment's chemistry over six weeks. Sediment that the animals had digested contained more dissolved nutrients and was less acidic than untouched sediment, changes that can help nearby corals grow.
choices: To describe research suggesting that sea cucumbers play a more active role on reefs than is often assumed
To describe research showing that sea cucumbers have little measurable effect on the sediment they digest
To explain how sea cucumbers move across the seafloor while searching for debris to eat
To argue that coral reefs cannot survive in any location where sea cucumbers are absent
explanation: The text states a common view (sea cucumbers are passive), pivots with 'however', and describes Varga's experiment, which found that the animals change sediment in ways that help corals. Choice A captures that correction.

B.why: You trusted 'describe research' and didn't check the result. Varga found clear changes in nutrients and acidity, which is the opposite of 'little measurable effect.'

C.why: You picked up on the detail about drifting across the seafloor. That detail is part of the old view the text corrects. The passage never explains how the animals move.

D.why: You went further than the evidence. The text says the changes 'can help' corals grow. It never claims that reefs cannot survive without sea cucumbers.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus: Before satellites, mapmakers charted entire countries using a method called triangulation. Surveyors first measured a single straight baseline on the ground with great care. From each end of that line, they sighted a distant landmark and recorded the angles. Because a triangle's unknown sides can be calculated from one side and two angles, each new triangle supplied a baseline for the next, extending the survey across hundreds of miles.
choices: To explain how triangulation let surveyors map large regions starting from one carefully measured line
To describe how surveyors decided which distant landmarks were most suitable for recording angles
To compare the accuracy of triangulation surveys with the accuracy of modern satellite mapping
To argue that triangulation produced maps too inaccurate to be useful across very large distances
explanation: The text walks through a process step by step: measure a baseline, sight landmarks, calculate the sides, and chain the triangles together. Choice A names the whole mechanism and what it achieved.

B.why: You chose one step instead of the whole process. The text mentions sighting landmarks but never explains how surveyors chose them.

C.why: This is the comparison trap. Satellites appear only as a time marker in the first sentence. The text explains one method and never compares accuracy.

D.why: You assumed the text evaluates the method. It only explains it, and it says triangulation extended surveys 'across hundreds of miles', which is the opposite of 'too inaccurate.'
